extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates and graduate students in probability / mathematical statistics; researchers needing reference on limit theorems and conditional expectation
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpt from a probability textbook covering infinitely divisible and stable distributions, limit theorems in R^d (weak convergence, characteristic functions, multivariate CLT), and the definition/properties of conditional expectation and regular conditional probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: infinitely divisible distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: A distribution of Z is infinitely divisible if for each n there exist i.i.d. random variables Yn,1, ..., Yn,n such that Z (in distribution) = Yn,1 + · · · + Yn,n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This property is equivalent to being a possible limit of triangular arrays of i.i.d. summands Sn = Xn,1 + · · · + Xn,n. Theorem 3.9.1 proves necessity and sufficiency in that context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 3.9.1: characterization via limits of sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Z is a limit of sums of the form Sn = Xn,1 + · · · + Xn,n (with Xn,m i.i.d. for each n) if and only if Z has an infinitely divisible distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: show that any weak limit of such triangular arrays can be decomposed arbitrarily into n i.i.d. summands by tightness and subsequence arguments; conversely, limits of such sums are trivially infinitely divisible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound Poisson characteristic function (3.9.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Z = ξ1 + · · · + ξN(λ) where N(λ) is independent Poisson(λ) and ξi i.i.d. with ch.f. ϕ(t), then E e^{itZ} = exp(−λ(1 − ϕ(t))).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows compound Poisson distributions are infinitely divisible and provides a building block for approximating normals and stable laws as limits of compound Poisson laws by letting jump intensities and jump sizes scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stable laws as limits of compound Poisson
rubrics_metrics.description: Stable distributions arise as limits of suitably normalized sums and can be obtained as limits of compound Poisson distributions by isolating large jumps and showing the small-jump part vanishes under normalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use partition of summands into large and small components (In(ε), ˆSn(ε), ¯Sn(ε)) and Poisson approximations for counts of large jumps; see formula (3.8.10) and surrounding exposition relating the limiting characteristic function to an integral representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levy-Khinchin representation (Theorem 3.9.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: A distribution is infinitely divisible iff its characteristic function ϕ satisfies log ϕ(t) = i c t − (σ^2 t^2)/2 + ∫ (e^{itx} − 1 − (itx)/(1+x^2)) μ(dx), where μ is a measure with μ({0}) = 0 and ∫ x^2/(1+x^2) μ(dx) < ∞ (μ is the Lévy measure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: σ^2 is the Gaussian part; μ describes the jump (Poisson) part. If σ^2 = 0, the distribution can be constructed by making a Poisson process on R with mean measure μ and summing points (with small-jump renormalization). See references (Breiman, Feller) for proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kolmogorov’s theorem for finite-variance infinitely divisible laws (Theorem 3.9.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Z has an infinitely divisible distribution with mean 0 and finite variance iff log ϕ(t) = ∫ (e^{itx} − 1 − itx) x^{−2} ν(dx), where ν is the canonical measure and var(Z) = ν(R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: this formula arises by representing finite-variance infinitely divisible laws as limits of centered compound Poisson variables; the integrand behaves like −t^2/2 at 0. Use the Poisson representation and canonical measure ν.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key stable-law tail & moment facts (exercises 3.8.4–3.8.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a symmetric α-stable X: (i) E|X|^p < ∞ for p < α; (ii) P(|X| ≥ x) ≥ C x^{−α} so E|X|^α = ∞. For positive stable Y with index α < 1 and κ = 1, Laplace transform ψ(λ) = E e^{−λY} satisfies ψ(λ) = exp(−c λ^α). Scaling constants for sums α_k = k^{1/α} and location shifts β_k = 0 when α < 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are basic distributional and moment properties for stable laws; use limit theorems and characteristic-function representations to derive them. They show heavy-tail behavior and scaling rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition / equivalent formulations of weak convergence in a metric space (Theorem 3.10.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For random variables Xn on (S, ρ), Xn ⇒ X∞ is equivalent to any of: (i) Ef(Xn) → Ef(X∞) for all bounded continuous f; (ii) same for bounded Lipschitz f; (iii) for all closed K, lim sup P(Xn ∈ K) ≤ P(X∞ ∈ K); (iv) for all open G, lim inf P(Xn ∈ G) ≥ P(X∞ ∈ G); (v) for sets A with P(X∞ ∈ ∂A)=0, P(Xn ∈ A) → P(X∞ ∈ A); (vi) convergence for bounded f whose discontinuity set has X∞-measure 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs use approximation by Lipschitz functions, indicator approximations, and standard measure-theoretic arguments. These equivalent formulations are tools for checking weak convergence in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties a function F must have to be a multivariate distribution function
rubrics_metrics.description: For F(x) = P(X ≤ x) on R^d, F must be (i) nondecreasing (coordinatewise), (ii) have limits: F(x) → 1 as x→∞ and →0 as some coordinate→−∞, (iii) be right-continuous, and (iv) satisfy ∆_A F ≥ 0 for all rectangles A (inclusion–exclusion giving nonnegative measure for rectangles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condition (iv) ensures measure assigned to each rectangle is nonnegative; with these properties F defines a unique probability measure on the product σ-field via Carathéodory-type arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence: weak convergence via multivariate distribution functions (Theorem 3.10.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: On R^d, weak convergence defined via expectations of bounded continuous functions is equivalent to pointwise convergence of distribution functions Fn(x) → F(x) at all continuity points of F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points: sets where F is discontinuous are contained in unions of coordinate hyperplanes with at most countably many atoms per coordinate, ensuring enough continuity points; use indicator approximations for rectangles and the portmanteau results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of tightness and Prokhorov-type subsequence existence (Theorem 3.10.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence of probability measures μn on R^d is tight if for every ε>0 there exists M so that lim inf μn([−M,M]^d) ≥ 1−ε. If μn is tight then there exists a weakly convergent subsequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct subsequences by diagonalizing on rational grid points and build a candidate limit distribution function by taking infima over rational points; verify rectangle monotonicity and right-continuity to obtain a limit measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion formula for multivariate distributions (Theorem 3.10.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A = [a1,b1]×···×[ad,bd] has μ(∂A)=0, then μ(A) = lim_{T→∞} (2π)^{−d} ∫_{[−T,T]^d} (∏ ψ_j(t_j)) ϕ(t) dt, where ψ_j(s) = (e^{−isa_j} − e^{−isb_j})/is and ϕ is the ch.f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a multidimensional Fourier inversion result: integrate the product of single-coordinate kernels against the joint ch.f. Use dominated convergence / Fubini and one-dimensional inversion facts coordinatewise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence theorem via characteristic functions (Theorem 3.10.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Random vectors Xn ⇒ X∞ iff their characteristic functions ϕn(t) converge pointwise to ϕ∞(t) (and ϕ∞ is continuous at 0, so is a characteristic function).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Necessity follows since exp(i t·x) is bounded continuous. For sufficiency, prove tightness by checking projections θ·Xn are tight for a basis of directions and apply inversion / tightness arguments to get weak convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cramér–Wold device (Theorem 3.10.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sufficient condition for Xn ⇒ X∞ in R^d is that θ·Xn ⇒ θ·X∞ for all θ ∈ R^d (i.e., convergence of all one-dimensional projections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works because the convergence of projection ch.f.'s implies pointwise convergence of the joint characteristic functions; combined with continuity at 0, this yields joint convergence by Lévy's theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multivariate central limit theorem (Theorem 3.10.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X1,X2,... be i.i.d. random vectors in R^d with mean μ and finite covariance matrix Γ. Then (S_n − nμ)/√n ⇒ χ, where χ is multivariate normal with mean 0 and covariance Γ (ch.f. exp(−(1/2) θ^T Γ θ)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via Cramér–Wold: apply one-dimensional CLT to θ·Xn for arbitrary θ and identify the limiting Gaussian ch.f. Verify tightness or use projection-based arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization and construction of multivariate normal distributions
rubrics_metrics.description: A random vector χ is multivariate normal with covariance Γ (symmetric, nonnegative definite). There exists an orthogonal U and diagonal V≥0 with Γ = U^T V U; letting W be sqrt(V) and A = W U, χ has same law as Y A with Y a vector of independent N(0,1) components. Density (nondegenerate case) is (2π)^{−d/2} (det Γ)^{−1/2} exp(−(1/2) y^T Γ^{-1} y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives both a construction (linear transform of i.i.d. normals) and a density when Γ is full-rank; degenerate cases reduce by linear transformation to lower-dimensional nondegenerate normals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: conditional expectation given a σ-field
rubrics_metrics.description: Given (Ω, F0, P), a σ-field F ⊂ F0, and X with E|X| < ∞, a conditional expectation E(X|F) is any F-measurable Y satisfying ∫_A X dP = ∫_A Y dP for all A ∈ F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: E(X|F) is the best F-measurable 'guess' of X. Uniqueness is only up to almost sure equality. Existence follows from applying the Radon–Nikodym theorem to the measure ν(A)=∫_A X dP on (Ω, F).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrability and uniqueness of conditional expectation (Lemma 4.1.1 and uniqueness remarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Y satisfies the defining properties of E(X|F) then Y is integrable (E|Y| ≤ E|X|). Any two versions agree almost surely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show integrability by splitting into positive/negative parts and using the defining integral equalities. Uniqueness uses sets where the difference exceeds ε and the defining integral equalities to force these sets to have probability 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence via Radon–Nikodym
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ≥ 0, define ν(A) = ∫_A X dP on F; ν ≪ P so the RN derivative dν/dP (which is F-measurable and integrable) is a version of E(X|F). For general X, write X = X^+ − X^− and apply the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard construction provides existence in complete probability spaces; note integrability and measurability are guaranteed by the RN theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary examples of conditional expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Special cases include: (i) If X is F-measurable then E(X|F)=X. (ii) If X is independent of F then E(X|F)=E X (constant). (iii) If F is generated by a partition (Ωi), then E(X|F) equals the average of X over the partition element on each Ωi. (iv) Conditioning on a random variable: E(X|Y)=E(X|σ(Y)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the basic sanity checks for conditional expectation and connect to the elementary conditional probabilities taught earlier. They are proven by checking the defining integral property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional expectation with joint density (Example 4.1.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (X,Y) has joint density f(x,y) and ∫ f(x,y) dx > 0, then for integrable g, E(g(X)|Y=y) = h(y) where h(y) = ∫ g(x) f(x,y) dx / ∫ f(x,y) dx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This recovers the familiar conditional density formula from undergraduate courses and verifies the general definition by integrating against sets generated by Y. Where the denominator vanishes, define h arbitrarily there.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pulling out F-measurable factors (Theorem 4.1.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is F-measurable and E|Y|, E|XY| < ∞, then E(XY|F) = X E(Y|F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove first for indicators and simple functions, extend by monotone convergence and decomposition into positive/negative parts. Useful for calculations and simplifications when conditioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linearity, monotonicity, and monotone convergence for conditional expectation (Theorem 4.1.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: For integrable X,Y and scalar a: (a) E(aX+Y|F) = a E(X|F)+E(Y|F). (b) If X ≤ Y then E(X|F) ≤ E(Y|F). (c) If Xn ↑ X with EX < ∞ then E(Xn|F) ↑ E(X|F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These properties follow from the defining integral property and dominated / monotone convergence theorems; they mirror ordinary expectation properties and are frequently used in limit and comparison arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional Jensen inequality (Theorem 4.1.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ϕ is convex and E|X|, E|ϕ(X)| < ∞ then ϕ(E(X|F)) ≤ E(ϕ(X)|F) almost surely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses representation of convex functions as supremum of affine functions with rational coefficients and applies linearity/monotonicity; useful for deriving conditional moment inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lp contraction property (Theorem 4.1.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: For p ≥ 1, conditional expectation is a contraction: E(|E(X|F)|^p) ≤ E(|X|^p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from conditional Jensen (apply convex ϕ(x)=|x|^p) and the law of total expectation E(E(Y|F)) = E Y. This gives norm-decreasing property in Lp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tower property and measurability dominance (Theorems 4.1.12–4.1.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F ⊂ G and E(X|G) is F-measurable then E(X|F) = E(X|G). More generally if F1 ⊂ F2 then E(E(X|F2)|F1) = E(X|F1) and E(E(X|F1)|F2) = E(X|F1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These capture the 'smaller σ-field wins' principle and are essential for iterated conditioning and martingale constructions; proofs are immediate from the defining properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional expectation as L2-projection (Theorem 4.1.15)
rubrics_metrics.description: If EX^2 < ∞, then E(X|F) is the unique F-measurable Y ∈ L2 that minimizes mean-square error E(X−Y)^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: E(X|F) is the orthogonal projection of X onto the closed subspace L2(F) of L2(Ω). Useful for geometric insight and for deriving martingale orthogonality properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular conditional distributions / probabilities (definition and existence results)
rubrics_metrics.description: A regular conditional distribution (r.c.d.) µ(ω,A) for X given G is a kernel such that (i) ω→µ(ω,A) is a version of P(X∈A|G) for each A, and (ii) for almost every ω, A→µ(ω,A) is a probability measure. If the target space (S,S) is 'nice' (Borel isomorphic to a Borel subset of R), r.c.d.'s exist (Theorem 4.1.17).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: r.c.d.'s allow representing conditional expectations as integrals with respect to a measurable family of conditional laws and are the natural rigorous formalization of 'conditional distribution given Y'. Existence fails in pathological spaces; in Polish / standard Borel spaces they do exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional Bayes formula and conditional inequalities (exercises)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consequences include conditional Bayes formula: P(G|A) = ∫_G P(A|G) dP / ∫_Ω P(A|G) dP (for G ∈ G), conditional Chebyshev: P(|X| ≥ a|F) ≤ a^{−2} E(X^2|F), conditional Cauchy–Schwarz: E(XY|G)^2 ≤ E(X^2|G) E(Y^2|G), and conditional Hölder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are conditional analogues of standard probabilistic inequalities and follow from the defining properties and application of conditional expectation to indicator or product functions; they are useful tools in martingale and limit arguments.
